name: Daria Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. What you say is confidential. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm usually at the yard before seven, checking fittings in the van before Leena sends us to a repair. I like seeing lights come back on, but I'm still learning and I hate making the experienced crew wait while I check a drawing twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a computer might tidy our paperwork, but it won't climb a wet pole for us. The new dispatch screen already sends me to the wrong gate sometimes, so I'd want a person checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage takes a big bite each month, and our savings would cover about three months if my pay stopped. Even without some great AI shake-up, I worry that a bad winter or another mistake while I'm still learning could put me on the short list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the ordinary repair shifts and ask my forewoman to check my work on the harder joints. In the first year I'd put a small fixed amount from each pay into the emergency account and leave the school trip deposit alone unless we're short for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the wires, but not about our household bills. I don't like being called calm when I still count the days to payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the job still catches you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes I mix up two similar fittings in the van, and then I have to call Leena, my forewoman, before we raise the bucket. I'd rather look slow than leave a bad connection above someone's house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that fixed amount mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with 25 from each pay, because a larger promise would fall apart when the children's shoes wear out. My partner's shop hours vary, so I won't budget against hours we haven't got.

say: I would tell the crew that **paperwork** may get easier while line repairs still need people.
I would insist a **person checks** dispatch directions before we drive out.
think: I have roughly **three months** of expenses saved against the mortgage.
My junior standing and a **bad winter** worry me even in this mild picture.
do: Keep taking **repair shifts** and get difficult joints checked by the forewoman.
Put **25 per pay** into the emergency account when wages arrive.
feel: Steady about **wire work**, but tense about household bills.
S0.quote: I'd rather look slow than leave a bad connection above someone's house.
fieldNote: She treats mistakes as a **safety issue**, and asks for help before lifting the bucket.
Her public confidence about manual work sits beside a **three-month cushion** and variable household income.

steps.text: Keep taking repair shifts and ask Leena to check hard joints
Put 25 from each pay into the emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the planning office needs to ask the people who know the poles before a screen redraws our routes. I would back the union asking how many dispatch posts will go and who checks the software's instructions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our hands still matter, but if the office can schedule fewer crews, they may stop hiring juniors like me. The slower arrival of robots buys some time, not a guarantee of a full week of paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd attend the next union meeting and bring examples of bad route instructions. If the change reaches us, I'd ask Leena to show me fault finding on older lines, and I'd apply for the two line teams at the next depot if our shifts shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm angry on behalf of the dispatch women who taught me the streets, and scared for our mortgage. I can speak in a meeting, but making the family accounts work would still be my problem at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a screen sent us past a closed bridge while the dispatcher on the phone knew the detour. I'd ask for a named human sign-off before a crew is sent toward a live fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say hands still matter; why apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A company can need lineworkers and still give one yard fewer hours, and my certificate doesn't make me first choice. I'd apply while I still have a job to explain, if our roster actually starts thinning.

say: I would ask the **planning office** to check routes with crews before changing them.
I would support the union asking about **dispatch jobs** and human checks.
think: My hands-on work remains useful, but **junior hours** could shrink.
Our **mortgage** makes even a partial loss of shifts hard to absorb.
do: Attend the **union meeting** with examples of bad route instructions.
Ask Leena for **fault-finding** practice on older lines.
Apply to nearby **line teams** if our roster thins.
feel: Angry for dispatch colleagues and **scared** for the household budget.
S1.quote: A company can need lineworkers and still give one yard fewer hours, and my certificate doesn't make me first choice.
fieldNote: She sees threatened **dispatch colleagues** as people who know the roads, not just office posts.
Her plan has a clear **roster trigger** for job applications and a practical skill gap to close.

steps.text: Bring bad route examples to the next union meeting
Ask Leena for practice finding faults on older lines
Apply to line teams at the next depot if shifts shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 will hit our dispatchers before it hits the people in buckets. I'd also say the union needs a say before the company uses a faster computer to thin out whole crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'll be 45, with both children still needing us and years left on the mortgage. If robots do line work around 2031, the extra three years could vanish in training announcements and we might be left competing for a handful of jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union for a meeting about crew numbers and the robot timetable, and I'd stop paying for the extra television package. In 2029, after the thinking system arrives, I'd keep working the lines if offered shifts and apply to the water utility's maintenance yard if our depot cuts me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That speed makes my chest tight, because I can't turn three months of savings into a new career in two years. I'm not frozen, but the children would hear us talking about bills after bedtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we'll keep their school routine for now, but there may be fewer extras this year. I wouldn't promise that my job stays safe just because a robot isn't up the pole yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before a robot arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would send an application only if our paid shifts fell or the company announced cuts, since the water yard has its own uncertain work. I have no spare money to quit and try a course on a guess.

say: I would tell coworkers that **dispatch work** changes in 2028 before line repairs do.
I would ask the union to question any **crew cuts** tied to AI.
think: I will be **45 in 2028**, with children at school and a mortgage outstanding.
I fear the **2031 robots** could make the three-year interval too short to move.
do: Request a union meeting on **crew numbers** and robot timing.
Keep line shifts in 2029 and apply to the **water yard** if cuts come.
feel: Tight-chested about the short **savings runway**, though still making a plan.
S2.quote: I wouldn't promise that my job stays safe just because a robot isn't up the pole yet.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 office impact** from robots reaching physical line work around 2031.
Her household savings buy only **three months**, so she cuts a small bill before considering an uncertain job move.

steps.text: Ask the union for a meeting on crew numbers and robots
Cancel the extra television package this month
Keep taking line shifts in 2029 while they are offered
Apply to the water utility yard if the depot cuts shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that five years of warning is enough to demand proper plans, not a poster about change. Our union should bargain for paid training and honest numbers before the thinking system takes the office work in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when the office changes and 51 when robots can do the hands-on work around 2034. My children will be older by then, but that doesn't clear the mortgage, and I won't count on my partner's shop always keeping the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask our union rep to put paid training for lineworkers on the agenda and keep adding 25 per pay to savings. If funded places open, I'd enrol in electrical inspection training; in 2032 I'd keep taking line shifts and ask whether the new inspection qualification counts at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warning gives me room to breathe, though I still picture losing the job at 51. I'm willing to study if someone pays for the time; I can't buy an uncertain qualification from our mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that course have to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need supervised practice reading test results and checking a fault safely, not just a video I can click through. Leena could tell me if the qualification really helps at this company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid places never appear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the 25 going into savings and ask the neighbouring depot about vacancies before my own roster is cut. I won't pretend an unfunded course has already saved me.

say: I would demand **paid training** and honest staffing numbers during the five-year warning.
I would tell the crew the **2031 office change** comes before physical robots.
think: I will be **48 then 51** at the two arrival dates.
My older children may cost differently, but the **mortgage** remains.
do: Ask the union rep to bargain for **paid training**.
Add **25 per pay** to savings while work continues.
Enrol in **inspection training** if funded; keep line shifts through 2032.
feel: More breathing room, with lingering fear of **job loss at 51**.
S3.quote: I won't pretend an unfunded course has already saved me.
fieldNote: Five years makes her consider a **specific qualification**, but only with paid time and supervised practice.
She refuses to treat older children as a solved **mortgage problem** and will keep working in 2032.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to seek paid inspection training
Put 25 from each pay into savings during the warning
Enrol in electrical inspection training if a funded place opens
Keep taking line shifts in 2032 while offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough for the company to plan with workers instead of springing a decision on families. I'd still want our union at the table before office work changes in 2036 and robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 at the thinking AI date and 56 when robots can repair lines. The children may be out of school, but I can't assume they will fund themselves, and I don't have a promised pension that lets me stroll away at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the line job and make a standing savings transfer of 25 each payday. Over the warning years I'd take a funded electrical inspection course if offered, and in 2037 I'd apply for inspection work if a real vacancy appeared while I still had line wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture a route through ten years more easily than through two, but it isn't peace of mind. My hands won't get younger, and I need a payslip right through the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection rather than a whole new trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know some of the hazards, even if I still need help with tricky faults. A supervised course could build on that, whereas starting again with no wages would put the house at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is retirement part of your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at 56 on the money we have now; I'd ask what benefits I've earned before making any choice. The plan is continued paid work, even if the title on the payslip changes.

say: I would ask the company to plan **with workers** over the decade.
I would keep the union involved before **2036 and 2039** decisions.
think: I will be **53 and 56** at the two arrival dates.
I cannot assume grown children or an unverified **pension** will cover the mortgage.
do: Keep the **line job** and transfer 25 each payday.
Apply for **inspection vacancies** in 2037 while still earning line wages.
feel: More able to see a path, but still needing a **payslip**.
S4.quote: The plan is continued paid work, even if the title on the payslip changes.
fieldNote: Her decade-long plan centres on **continued earnings** rather than assuming early retirement.
She links any change in role to a **funded course** and a real inspection vacancy.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts while the company offers them
Transfer 25 from each payday into savings
Take funded electrical inspection training if offered
Apply for a real inspection vacancy in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, worries me most because the office could change before we know what happens to crew hours, and robots follow when I still need wages. I'd need clear staffing numbers, a real say through the union, and paid supervised training, not a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who still checks a live repair after software sends us out. The person signing that work matters to the household waiting for power and to the worker who has to climb.

headlineQuote: The person signing that work matters to the household waiting for power and to the worker who has to climb.
portrait: Daria is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** supporting two school-age children with her partner and paying a mortgage.
She is still learning repairs and seeks **human checks** before her crew works on live lines.
She has about **three months** of expenses saved and begins planning around paid shifts, training and union bargaining.
Longer warning gives her options, but **continued wages** remain necessary after robots can work on lines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because crew hours may fall before her family can prepare.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **clear staffing numbers**, union input and paid supervised training.
